faq.q: What makes a B&B genuinely biker-friendly in Scotland?
faq.a: Look for secure covered parking (garage or locked outbuilding), dedicated drying facilities for wet gear, flexible meal times for late arrivals, and hosts who understand touring schedules don't always run to plan. Ground-floor room access is a bonus when hauling panniers.

faq.q: When is the best time to tour Scotland on a motorcycle?
faq.a: May through September offers the best weather, though you should still pack for all conditions. May, early June, and September are ideal – decent weather with fewer tourists and campervans clogging single-track roads compared to peak summer.

faq.q: How much should I budget for B&B accommodation in Scotland?
faq.a: Expect £60-80 per night in the Borders and less touristy areas, £90-130 in the Highlands and popular spots, and £150+ on Skye during summer. Booking early secures better rates, and most prices include a full Scottish breakfast.

faq.q: Do I need to book accommodation in advance for a Scottish tour?
faq.a: Book the first and last nights plus anywhere really popular (Skye, Fort William, NC500 route in summer) well ahead – sometimes months in advance for peak season. Leave middle sections flexible so you can adjust for weather and spontaneous detours.

faq.q: What daily mileage should I plan when touring the Scottish Highlands?
faq.a: Plan for 150-200 miles maximum per day in the Highlands, even if you could cover much more elsewhere. Single-track sections, sheep, tractors, tourists, and the twisting nature of Highland roads all slow progress, but that's part of the experience.

content:
Finding the Perfect Biker-Friendly B&B in Scotland

I've spent years touring Scotland on two wheels, and I can tell you right now: where you rest your head at night makes or breaks a touring trip. A proper biker-friendly B&B isn't just about a bed – it's about secure parking for your pride and joy, somewhere to dry your kit after riding through Highland rain, and hosts who don't bat an eyelid when you turn up looking like you've wrestled with the A82 in a thunderstorm.

Scotland's got some of the finest riding roads in Britain, but it's also got weather that can turn from glorious sunshine to biblical downpour in the time it takes to pull over and check your map. That's why I'm sharing the B&Bs I actually use when I'm touring north of the border – places where I know my bike's safe, my gear will dry overnight, and I'll get a breakfast big enough to fuel a full day tackling the twists and turns of the Highlands.

What Makes a B&B Genuinely Biker-Friendly?

Before I dive into specific recommendations, let me tell you what I look for. I've stayed in dozens of B&Bs across Scotland, and the difference between "motorcycle friendly" and genuinely understanding riders is massive.

First up: secure, covered parking. I don't care how quiet the village is – I want my bike somewhere I can see it or locked away properly. The best places have a garage or secure outbuilding. Ground-floor room access is brilliant too, especially when you're hauling panniers and a tank bag up narrow Victorian staircases after a 300-mile day.

Next: drying facilities. Scotland's weather is spectacular, but it's also spectacularly wet. I need radiators or a drying room for waterproofs, boots, and gloves. Nothing ruins a morning faster than pulling on damp gloves before tackling the NC500.

Flexible meal times matter as well. When you're chasing daylight in October or you've spent an extra hour photographing the view from the Rest and Be Thankful, arriving after standard dinner service shouldn't mean going hungry. The best hosts either feed you late or point you toward decent local takeaways that'll deliver.

A genuinely biker-friendly B&B understands that riders need secure parking, proper drying facilities, and hosts who get that touring schedules don't always run to plan – these basics matter more than fancy amenities.

The Scottish Highlands: My Top Picks

The Clansman, Fort Augustus

Right on the southern tip of Loch Ness, The Clansman has sorted me out more times than I can count. Graham and Sue run it, and they're both riders themselves – Graham's got a gorgeous R1200GS that he tours Europe on. That means they genuinely understand what we need.

The locked garage holds six bikes comfortably, and there's a proper drying room with heated rails. The rooms are nothing fancy, but they're clean, warm, and the beds are excellent. After a long day riding the A87 or exploring the roads around Glen Affric, that matters more than thread count.

Fort Augustus sits perfectly for exploring the western Highlands. You're forty minutes from the Skye bridge, an hour from Applecross (if you're taking the Bealach na Bà, which you absolutely should), and it's a brilliant base for tackling sections of the NC500 without committing to the full circuit.

The breakfast is proper fuel: full Scottish with black pudding, tattie scones, and eggs from their neighbour's chickens. Sue understands that cereal doesn't cut it when you're planning a run up to Durness and back.

Mackay's Rooms, Durness

Up in the far northwest, Mackay's has become my go-to when I'm riding the top section of the NC500. It's not technically a B&B – more of a guest house – but Alan Mackay treats bikers brilliantly.

The bike parking is in a walled yard round the back with CCTV, and Alan's got a workshop if you need to do basic maintenance. I've tightened chain tension there more than once after the twisting roads from Tongue. He's got a decent basic toolkit and doesn't mind you using it.

Durness itself is tiny, but the location is unbeatable. You're fifteen minutes from Smoo Cave, twenty from the Cape Wrath ferry (worth the trip if you've got an adventure bike), and the coastal roads around here are simply stunning. The ride from Durness to Tongue via the A838 is one of my favourites in all of Scotland – sweeping bends with sea views that'll have you stopping every few miles.

The rooms are basic but spotless, and breakfast is continental-style – perfect if you want to get an early start chasing the morning light.

The Torridon Inn, by Loch Torridon

This one's a proper inn rather than a B&B, but I'm including it because it's exceptional for bikers. The setting is jaw-dropping – right on the loch with the mountains rising behind – and the staff have been looking after touring riders for decades.

They've got a dedicated motorcycle parking area with chains and ground anchors if you're carrying your own lock (I always do – you can grab decent disc locks from SportsBikeShop before your trip). The drying room is industrial-strength; I've had soaking wet textiles bone-dry overnight.

The food's a step up from standard B&B fare too. After riding the Glen Torridon road or tackling the Bealach na Bà from the Applecross side, their venison stew and a pint of local ale is exactly what you need. Book ahead though – this place is popular with bikers, cyclists, and hikers.

The Scottish Borders: Hidden Gems

Sunnyside Guest House, Melrose

Down in the Borders, Sunnyside doesn't look like much from the outside, but Karen who runs it is brilliant with bikers. Her husband rides, so she gets it – the secure garage, the drying room, the flexible breakfast times.

Melrose is perfectly placed for exploring the Borders roads, which I reckon are underrated by most touring riders. Everyone charges north to the Highlands, but the roads around here – the B6356 through Bowhill, the route over to St Mary's Loch – are fantastic riding. Less traffic, great surfaces, and the scenery's beautiful even if it's not as dramatic as the Highlands.

The rooms are comfortable, the WiFi actually works (not always guaranteed in rural Scotland), and Karen does brilliant home baking. Her tablet shortbread has fueled many an afternoon ride.

Caddon View, Innerleithen

Stuart and Helen at Caddon View welcome bikers warmly, and they've invested in proper facilities. The motorcycle shelter is covered and secure, with power points if you need to charge a battery or heated kit.

Innerleithen's a great base for exploring the Borders and makes a good stop if you're riding between England and the Highlands. The A708 from here to Moffat is a gorgeous road – twisting through hills, past St Mary's Loch, with barely any traffic midweek.

The breakfast is substantial, and they'll do packed lunches if you ask the night before. Useful when you're planning a full day's ride and don't want to faff about finding lunch in the middle of nowhere.

The Islands: Worth the Ferry Crossing

The Bosville Hotel, Portree, Skye

Skye's not short of accommodation, but finding genuinely biker-friendly places that aren't extortionate can be tricky. The Bosville sorts both issues. They've got secure parking (crucial in busy Portree), good drying facilities, and the rates are reasonable for Skye.

Portree makes a brilliant base for exploring the island. You can ride the Trotternish loop in a morning, head down to the Cuillin in the afternoon, or make the run out to Neist Point. The roads on Skye range from brilliant (the Trotternish ridge road) to slightly terrifying (some of the single-track stuff near Elgol), but they're all memorable.

Fair warning: Skye gets rammed in summer. Book well ahead, and if you can tour in May, early June, or September, you'll have a much better time. The weather's decent enough, and you won't be stuck behind campervans doing 30mph on every single-track section.

The Arran Lodge, Brodick, Isle of Arran

Arran's often overlooked by touring riders heading to the Highlands, but it's a cracking island for motorcycling. The coast road circuit is about 60 miles of varied riding – everything from fast sweepers on the east coast to tighter bends climbing over the String Road from Brodick to Blackwaterfoot.

The Arran Lodge has dedicated motorcycle parking, and the hosts are used to bikers coming off the ferry. Brodick's convenient being right by the ferry terminal – you can be off the boat and checked in within minutes.

The island's small enough to explore thoroughly in a day or two, making it perfect for a quick touring break or as part of a larger Scottish trip. I've used it as a stop on rides from the islands to the Highlands, breaking up the journey and enjoying some brilliant riding without the traffic you get on the mainland.

Essential Tips for Booking and Staying

Right, some practical advice from years of touring Scotland. First: always phone to book rather than using online booking systems. Have a quick chat with whoever answers – you'll get a feel for whether they actually want bikers or just tick a box on booking websites. Ask specific questions about bike parking and drying facilities.

When you arrive, take five minutes to sort your kit properly. Get wet stuff onto radiators or drying racks immediately – don't dump it in a heap and hope it'll dry overnight. It won't. Scotland's damp even when it's not actually raining.

Most B&Bs want you out by 10am, which is fine when you're touring, but check if you can leave luggage if you're doing a big loop and coming back. Some places are flexible, others aren't. Knowing beforehand saves awkward conversations when you're trying to leave.

Pack light if you can. I know, I know – we all want options. But hauling three panniers and a massive tail pack up narrow B&B staircases gets old fast. Before you set off, check out our packing checklist to streamline what you're carrying. You really don't need four pairs of jeans for a week's tour.

Finally: tip if service has been good. B&B hosts work hard, and the ones who genuinely look after bikers deserve recognition. I usually leave a tenner if I've stayed two nights and everything's been spot on. It's appreciated, and you'll be remembered warmly if you return.

Planning Your Scottish Touring Trip

When you're building an itinerary, think about realistic daily distances. Scotland's roads are brilliant but they're not fast. Single-track sections, sheep in the road, tractors, tourists – they all slow you down. I plan for 150-200 miles maximum per day in the Highlands, even though I could easily cover 400 miles in that time down in England.

Use our route building tool to map out your trip, but build in flexibility. Weather changes plans in Scotland. I've had trips where the forecast's been perfect and I've been rained on for three days straight. Equally, I've expected terrible weather and got sunshine for a week.

Book accommodation for the first and last nights, plus anywhere really popular (Skye, Fort William, anywhere on the NC500 in summer). Leave the middle sections flexible so you can adjust based on weather, how you're feeling, and what takes your fancy. Some of my best touring memories have come from unplanned detours and spontaneous decisions to stay somewhere an extra night.

Weather-wise, May through September is your best bet, but even then pack for all conditions. I carry full waterproofs even on sunny days, because Scottish weather can turn in minutes. Check our essential touring gear guide for kit recommendations, but at minimum: decent waterproofs, thermal layers, and proper gloves. Heated gear's brilliant if your bike can handle it – I've got heated grips and a vest, and they're game-changers on cold Highland mornings.

What to Expect: Costs and Booking

B&B prices in Scotland vary wildly. In the Borders or less touristy areas, you're looking at £60-80 per night for a decent double room with breakfast. In the Highlands, popular spots, or islands, expect £90-130. Skye in summer? You might pay £150+ unless you book early.

Many places want two-night minimum stays in peak season, particularly on Skye and the NC500 route. Frustrating when you're touring, but understandable from their perspective. Book ahead for summer (April onwards for popular spots), but you can often rock up and find somewhere outside peak season.

Breakfast is almost always included – full Scottish, which is basically a full English with tattie scones and sometimes haggis. It's substantial fuel for riding. Some places offer packed lunches for £6-8, worth it on long riding days when you don't fancy stopping somewhere touristy and overpriced.

My Practical Takeaway

Scotland's an incredible place to tour on a motorcycle, and staying at proper biker-friendly B&Bs makes the whole experience better. You'll meet other riders, get local knowledge on roads and conditions, and actually rest properly instead of worrying about your bike or wearing damp kit the next morning.

The places I've recommended aren't fancy or Instagram-worthy. They're practical, welcoming, and run by people who understand what touring riders need. That's worth more than a four-poster bed and posh toiletries every single time.

Start by picking one or two destinations you really want to ride, book accommodation there, then build your route around them. Use the flexibility of B&Bs – most hosts are brilliant at suggesting local routes, warning you about road conditions, and generally making sure you get the most out of the area. That local knowledge is gold.

Get your bike ready, book a couple of nights somewhere on this list, and go ride Scotland properly. The roads are waiting, and I promise you – with the right places to stay, it'll be a trip you'll remember for years.
